meta.title: Russian — Sounds and spelling
meta.subtitle: 27 cards on how the letters are read: unstressed vowels, hard and soft, ь and ъ, final consonants — after the alphabet, beside TORFL A1
meta.desc: How Russian is read once the letters are known: 27 notes, one card each — 9 on the vowels (what о, а, е and я become without the stress; ё, ю, ы and у; и and е after ж, ш and ц), 12 on consonant letters and groups (ь and ъ, the vowel letters that begin with a [j], й, г read as в in -ого and -его, ч in что, щ, ж and ш, ц, the ending -ться, х, р) and 6 rules of spelling (the six letters that look Latin and are not, the stress mark, hard and soft consonants and the vowel letters that show them, a voiced consonant at the end of a word, two consonants together, a consonant that is written and not said). The front shows the letters. The back gives the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet and the English sound it resembles, the source's own sentence where there is a rule, and words of the TORFL A1 deck with a speaker beside each, the letters picked out, A1's stress mark and the word's own transcription. Say the word, then press the speaker and compare. Of TORFL A1's 549 notes, 281 have an unstressed о or а, 185 a soft sign, 29 end in a voiced consonant that is read voiceless, and 424 hold one of В, Н, Р, С, У, Х. THE ORDER is the look-alike letters and the stress mark, the vowels, the consonants, then the other rules. At the default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 3 days; it follows the alphabet deck and is meant to be studied beside TORFL A1, not finished first. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: no description was written for this deck. Each sound and each English comparison is a cell of the first page named below, with that page's own labels (RP, American, Scottish, Australian English for the accent meant; "for some dialects"); the й and р rows and the look-alike letters are cells of the second; each rule is a sentence or a note of the page it comes from, with a cut marked […]. The small labels over a row (stressed, unstressed, last in the word) say where the letter stands in the words listed under it; each of those words carries the transcription that shows the sound. The letters that sound much as an English speaker expects have no card here; each has one in the alphabet deck. The example sentences of the word decks print no stress, as they were written: the stress of a word is on its own card. The speaker is your device's Russian voice reading the example word, so a device without one is silent. — Sounds and English comparisons: Wikipedia, “Help:IPA/Russian”, revision 1383914368 of 2026-11-05. Letters, the two signs, hard and soft, the stress mark: Wikipedia, “Russian alphabet”, revision 1381885718 of 2026-10-25. Silent consonants, -ться, stress: Wikipedia, “Russian phonology”, revision 1385867680 of 2026-11-15 (all CC BY-SA 4.0). Transcriptions: English Wiktionary, via kaikki.org (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words, stress and meanings: the TORFL A1 deck on this shelf (English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Name: the stress mark
fields.Says: The only diacritic, in the proper sense, is the acute accent ⟨◌́⟩ […], which marks stress on a vowel […]. Although Russian word stress is often unpredictable and can fall on different syllables in different forms of the same word, the diacritic accent is used only in dictionaries, children's books, resources for foreign-language learners […]. — Stress in Russian is phonemic and therefore unpredictable. It may fall on any syllable, and can vary drastically in similar or related words.

fields.Letters: а я · э е · ы и · о ё · у ю
fields.Name: hard and soft consonants
fields.Says: Most consonants can represent both "soft" (palatalized, represented in the IPA with a ⟨ʲ⟩) and "hard" consonant phonemes. If consonant letters are followed by vowel letters, the soft/hard quality of the consonant depends on whether the vowel is meant to follow "hard" consonants ⟨а, о, э, у, ы⟩ or "soft" consonants ⟨я, ё, е, ю, и⟩. A soft sign ⟨ь⟩ indicates palatalization of the preceding consonant without adding a vowel.

fields.Name: мягкий знак, the soft sign
fields.Says: The soft sign, ⟨ь⟩, in most positions acts like a "silent front vowel" and indicates that the preceding consonant is palatalized (except for always-hard ж, ш, ц) and the following vowel (if present) is iotated […]. This is important as palatalization is phonemic in Russian. For example, брат [brat] ('brother') contrasts with брать [bratʲ] ('to take').
fields.Examples:

брать[bratʲ]to take

семья́[sʲɪˈm⁽ʲ⁾ja]family

fields.Name: твёрдый знак, the hard sign
fields.Says: The hard sign, ⟨ъ⟩, acts like a "silent back vowel" that separates a succeeding "soft vowel" (⟨е, ё, ю, я⟩, but not ⟨и⟩) from a preceding consonant, invoking implicit iotation of the vowel with a distinct /j/ glide. Today it is used mostly to separate a prefix ending with a hard consonant from the following root.
fields.Examples:
as in
есть[jesʲtʲ]to eat
съесть[sjesʲtʲ]to eat

fields.Name: two consonants together
fields.Says: Consonants in consonant clusters are assimilated in voicing if the final consonant in the sequence is an obstruent (except [v, vʲ]). All consonants become voiceless if the final consonant is voiceless or voiced if the final consonant is voiced.

fields.Name: a consonant that is written and not said
fields.Says: Clusters of three or more consonants are frequently simplified, usually through syncope of one of them, especially in casual pronunciation. […] The orthographic combination ⟨вств⟩ is pronounced [stv] in the words здра́вствуй(те) [ˈzdrastvʊj(tʲe)] 'hello', чу́вство [ˈt͡ɕustvə] 'feeling' […]. — There are a handful of words in which consonants which have long since ceased to be pronounced even in careful pronunciation are still spelled, e.g., the 'l' in солнце [ˈsontsɨ] ('sun').
